narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 65% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. In practical terms, the review treated first-time failure as more likely than passing, and that risk was high enough to justify rejection.

The most influential factor was your third-year class standing. You were in the second decile, well below the average accepted student, who was around the sixth decile. This was the main reason the prediction moved toward bar failure. Your LSAT score of 38 was slightly above the accepted-student average of about 37.18, and your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 was above the average of about 3.23. Both of these factors worked in your favor and pushed toward passing. However, their positive influence was ranked below your third-year standing and was not strong enough to outweigh it. That is why the overall prediction still favored failure.

To strengthen a future application, focus on evidence of improved academic performance, especially in advanced or upper-level coursework. Consider retaking the LSAT only if practice results show a meaningful gain, and seek admissions or bar-readiness advising before reapplying. You may also consider delaying reapplication until you can present a clearer record of readiness for law school and bar study.
